Writers Guild of America member Steven Binder shows his approval as he votes Tuesday in Beverly Hills, California. It's unclear how soon new episodes of scripted programs will start appearing, because production won't begin until scripts are completed, the AP reported. It will take at least four weeks for producers to get the first post-strike episodes of comedies back on the air; dramas will take six to eight weeks, the AP said. Verrone said the WGA achieved two of three goals through negotiations with the studios.  Watch Verrone explain what he thinks the strike accomplished » . The first goal relates to writers' "jurisdiction" in new media, Verrone said, meaning that any content written by guild members specifically for new media, such as the Internet or cell phones, will be covered by their contract. The second goal relates to reuse of content in new media, Verrone said. The agreement bases payment for reuses on a distributor's gross formula for residuals, "so that when they get paid, we get paid," he said. It is the "first time in our history that a new delivery system pays on a residual formula superior to the prior existing system," Verrone said. The third goal, which Verrone said the guild did not achieve, was to shore up writers' shares of the revenue from animation and reality television. "Giving up animation and reality was a heartbreaking thing for me personally," he said. "But it was more important that we make a deal that benefited the membership, the town as a whole, that got people back to work and that solved the biggest problems in new media." # Writers Guild Strike Ends After 100 Days

More than 92 percent of Writers Guild of America members voted to end their 100-day strike, allowing writers to return to work Wednesday under a new three-year deal. The overwhelming support reflected the membership's readiness to resume work after more than three months of picketing that brought much of Hollywood's production to a standstill.

The strike began on November 5 after negotiations collapsed over how writers are compensated for the use of their material on the Internet, new media, and DVDs. As audiences increasingly shifted toward digital platforms, writers argued that existing compensation structures failed to account for the growing importance of these emerging revenue streams, making the dispute a defining battle over the future of the industry.

While celebrating the resolution, WGA West president Patric Verrone acknowledged the deal fell short of members' hopes but called it the best agreement the guild had negotiated in 30 years. His measured assessment recognized both the compromises writers had to accept and the significant gains they secured after a prolonged and costly work stoppage.

Industry leaders on the other side of the table echoed the sense of accomplishment. CBS CEO Leslie Moonves described the outcome as a fair deal in which everyone won and that fairly recognized the contributions writers make to the industry. His comments signaled a desire to move past the tensions of the strike and restore stable working relationships across Hollywood.

Beyond returning writers to their desks, the end of the strike ensured that the 80th Academy Awards ceremony on February 24 could proceed as the usual fully scripted event. The resolution came just in time to preserve one of the entertainment world's most prestigious occasions, sparing it from the disruptions that had already affected other awards shows during the walkout.

# Los Angeles, California

Los Angeles, often abbreviated as LA, is the largest city in the state of California and the second-most populous city in the United States. Located in Southern California along the Pacific coast, it is known for its Mediterranean climate, ethnic diversity, and sprawling metropolitan area.

## History and Growth

Founded in 1781 by Spanish settlers, Los Angeles grew from a small agricultural community into a global metropolis. The discovery of oil in the late 19th century and the rise of the film industry in the early 20th century transformed the city into an economic powerhouse. Today, LA is home to nearly four million residents within the city limits and over eighteen million in the greater metropolitan region.

## Entertainment Capital

Los Angeles is world-famous as the entertainment capital of the world. Hollywood, a neighborhood within the city, has been the center of the American film industry for more than a century. The iconic Hollywood Sign, the Walk of Fame, and numerous movie studios attract millions of tourists each year. Beyond film, LA is also a major hub for music, television, and digital media.

## Culture and Attractions

The city offers an incredible array of cultural attractions and activities. Visitors can explore world-class museums like the Getty Center and LACMA, relax on famous beaches such as Venice and Santa Monica, or enjoy the vibrant culinary scene shaped by countless cultures. The diverse neighborhoods, from Koreatown to Little Tokyo, reflect the city's rich multicultural identity.

## Climate and Lifestyle

Los Angeles enjoys warm, sunny weather for most of the year, contributing to its relaxed, outdoor-oriented lifestyle. This pleasant climate supports an active culture centered around fitness, wellness, and enjoying the natural beauty of nearby mountains, beaches, and deserts.

## Conclusion

With its unique blend of natural beauty, cultural richness, and economic influence, Los Angeles remains one of the most dynamic and influential cities in the world. Whether for its entertainment legacy, diverse population, or endless attractions, California's City of Angels continues to captivate people from all walks of life.

# Writers Guild Ends 100-Day Strike, Hollywood Prepares to Return to Work

**Writers vote overwhelmingly to end walkout that cost California economy billions**

LOS ANGELES (CNN) -- Members of the Writers Guild of America voted overwhelmingly Tuesday to end their 100-day strike, clearing the way for thousands of film and television writers to return to work and bringing an end to a labor dispute that paralyzed Hollywood and cost the local economy billions of dollars.

The guild announced that 92.5 percent of members who cast ballots voted to lift the strike order, allowing writers to return to their jobs as early as Wednesday. A separate vote on whether to formally ratify the new contract will take place over the coming weeks.

"The strike is over," WGA West President Patric Verrone told cheering members. "Our membership has spoken. This was not a strike we wanted, but one we had to conduct in order to win jurisdiction and establish appropriate residuals for the new-media market."

The three-year contract gives writers jurisdiction over content produced for the Internet and establishes a formula for compensating writers when their work is streamed or downloaded online -- issues that were at the heart of the walkout that began November 5.

## A Landmark Deal for the Digital Age

Union leaders characterized the agreement as a critical victory that positions writers for an entertainment landscape increasingly shaped by digital distribution.

"For the first time, we have established that writers will share in the revenues generated when their work is distributed over the Internet," said Michael Winship, president of the WGA East. "This is the future of our industry, and we secured a foothold in it."

The deal includes provisions for writers to receive a percentage of revenue from streaming programs, along with payments for content distributed through digital downloads.

## Studios Welcome Return to Production

Studio executives and representatives from the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers expressed relief that production could resume.

"We are pleased that the parties have reached an agreement that recognizes the enormous economic potential of new media while allowing our industry to get back to work," an AMPTP spokesman said in a statement. "This settlement respects the value of writers while giving companies the flexibility to grow the business in a changing marketplace."

One studio executive, speaking about the road ahead, said the focus now turns to recovery. "Everyone lost during this strike -- writers, studios, and the tens of thousands of workers who depend on this industry," the executive said. "Now the important thing is to rebuild and move forward together."

## Counting the Cost

The strike took a heavy toll on the entertainment industry and the broader Los Angeles economy. Economists estimated losses exceeding $2 billion, affecting not only writers but also caterers, drivers, set builders and countless other workers whose livelihoods depend on production.

Late-night talk shows were forced into reruns before eventually returning without their writing staffs. Prime-time television schedules were decimated, and the strike raised uncertainty over award shows, including the Golden Globes, which was reduced to a news conference.

## Looking Ahead

With writers heading back to work, attention now shifts to how quickly the industry can recover. Many scripted series are expected to resume production within days, though some shows may not return until the fall.

The settlement also sets the stage for upcoming negotiations with the Screen Actors Guild, whose contract expires later this year -- a talks that many in the industry will watch closely.

For now, writers expressed cautious optimism as they prepared to return to their keyboards.

"We stood together, and that solidarity made this deal possible," Verrone said. "Now it's time to get back to telling stories."

*CNN's entertainment unit contributed to this report.*

# WGA Strike Ends After 100 Days as Writers Secure Landmark New Media Deal

*Hollywood's screenwriters return to work following a three-month walkout that reshaped how creative talent is compensated in the digital age.*

After 100 days on the picket lines, members of the Writers Guild of America voted overwhelmingly to end their strike in February 2008, bringing to a close one of the most consequential labor disputes in modern entertainment history. The walkout, which began on November 5, 2007, brought television production to a standstill, disrupted late-night programming, and cost the Los Angeles economy an estimated $2 billion.

The strike centered on a single dominant concern: how writers would be compensated as their work migrated from traditional broadcast and home video to the rapidly expanding world of internet distribution.

## The Core Dispute: New Media Residuals

Residuals—the ongoing payments writers receive when their work is reused—had long been a cornerstone of guild compensation. But the explosive growth of streaming and digital downloads created new revenue streams that existing contracts failed to address. The WGA argued that studios were building lucrative online businesses while writers received little or nothing for content distributed through these channels.

The guild pursued three primary objectives regarding new media:

**1. Compensation for Streaming (Ad-Supported) Content**
The WGA sought residuals for television shows and films streamed online, particularly free, advertising-supported programming that studios were increasingly using to monetize their libraries. Writers wanted a share of the advertising revenue these platforms generated.

**2. Compensation for Paid Digital Downloads**
The guild demanded an improved formula for electronic sell-through and paid downloads (such as programs purchased through iTunes), arguing that the existing home-video residual rate—widely regarded as inadequate—should not be simply carried over to the digital marketplace.

**3. Coverage of Content Made for New Media**
The WGA wanted jurisdiction over original content created specifically for the internet, ensuring that writers producing web-based programming would be covered by guild protections and compensation standards.

## What the Writers Achieved

The final agreement, negotiated with the Alliance of Motion Picture and Television Producers (AMPTP), delivered mixed but historically significant results:

**Streaming residuals — Partial victory.** The writers won residuals for ad-supported streaming, but with an important caveat. The deal permitted studios a free "promotional window"—an initial period (17 or 24 days depending on the platform) during which content could be streamed without any residual payment. After that window, writers would receive a fixed payment in the first two years, transitioning to a percentage-based formula (approximately 2 percent of distributor's gross) in subsequent years. This established the crucial principle that streaming had value writers were entitled to share, even if the immediate rates were modest.

**Jurisdiction over new-media content — Achieved.** Perhaps the most durable win was securing WGA coverage for original content produced for the internet. This established the guild's authority over emerging forms of programming and ensured writers working in new formats would fall under union protection—a foundation that proved vital as streaming platforms later commissioned vast quantities of original material.

**Digital download rates — Limited success.** The writers made the least headway on paid downloads. The agreement essentially maintained rates closely tied to the existing home-video formula rather than establishing the substantially higher percentage the guild had originally sought. This was widely viewed as the area where the WGA conceded the most.

## The Significance of the Settlement

While the financial gains were incremental, industry observers regarded the establishment of principle as the strike's most important legacy. By forcing studios to acknowledge that internet distribution constituted a compensable revenue stream, the WGA laid groundwork that would shape future negotiations—including subsequent contract battles as streaming became the dominant force in entertainment.

WGA leadership framed the outcome as a foundation to build upon rather than a complete triumph. "We came together in a way that has changed our union forever," guild leaders told members, acknowledging that the deal was imperfect but represented meaningful progress in an entirely new economic landscape.

For the studios, the settlement provided cost certainty and returned writers to work, allowing the industry to salvage what remained of the television season and resume feature production.

The 2008 strike ultimately marked the entertainment industry's first serious reckoning with the digital transformation of media—a reckoning that would echo through labor negotiations for years to come.

Verrone praised the solidarity of the rank-and-file writers who walked picket lines outside studios throughout the dispute. "The unity of this membership was extraordinary. Writers who had never met one another became a community on those picket lines."

Michael Winship, president of the Writers Guild of America, East, echoed that sentiment, emphasizing that the outcome established important precedents for the future.

"For the first time, we have jurisdiction and compensation in new media that reflects where this industry is heading," Winship said. "That's what this fight was about — making sure writers share in the future of their own work, not just the past."

Winship added that the East and West branches had operated in lockstep throughout the negotiations. "This was a coast-to-coast effort. Our members in New York and Los Angeles stood as one, and that made all the difference."

For the studios, the resolution brought relief after months of stalled production and mounting financial pressure.

"We're pleased that our writers are coming back to work," said Leslie Moonves, chief executive of CBS Corporation, who had played a role in brokering the final stages of the talks. "This is a fair deal that recognizes the value writers bring while allowing our industry to move forward. Everybody is better off when we're making great content and getting it to audiences."

Moonves acknowledged the toll the strike had taken. "It was a difficult period for everyone — for the writers, for the companies, and certainly for all the people whose livelihoods depend on this business. Now it's time to get back to work."

Industry observers said the return of writers would allow television networks to begin restoring their schedules, though it would take time for scripted programming to ramp back up to full capacity. Late-night programs were expected to resume production quickly, while episodic dramas and comedies faced a longer path back to the air.

The strike underscored the tensions gripping an entertainment industry in the midst of a transition to digital distribution, a shift that has redefined how audiences consume content and how the people who create it are compensated.

For the writers now heading back to their keyboards, the mood was one of cautious optimism. As Verrone put it, "The pens are down no longer. It's time to tell stories again."

# Writers Strike Ends as Guild Members Approve New Contract

**LOS ANGELES** — Hollywood's screenwriters voted overwhelmingly to end their 100-day work stoppage, clearing the way for late-night talk shows to return immediately and scripted television production to resume within weeks.

Members of the Writers Guild of America approved the deal to lift the strike, with 92.5 percent voting in favor of ending the walkout that began in early November. The vote, tallied from both the guild's eastern and western branches, reflected broad support among the roughly 10,500 members for the tentative agreement negotiated with studios and producers.

## Digital Residuals at Heart of Dispute

The central issue driving the strike was compensation for content distributed over the internet and other new-media platforms. Writers had sought a greater share of revenue as studios increasingly streamed programs online and sold episodes through digital downloads.

Under the terms of the new three-year contract, writers secured jurisdiction over content created for the internet and established a formula for residual payments on programs streamed and sold through digital outlets. Guild leaders characterized the gains in new-media compensation as a significant victory that would protect writers as the industry shifts toward online distribution.

## Production Timeline

Late-night programs, which rely on topical monologues written fresh each day, were expected to return to the air almost immediately, some within days of the vote.

Scripted prime-time series faced a longer road back. Industry observers estimated that most dramas and comedies would need four to eight weeks before new episodes reached viewers, as writers returned to rooms, scripts were completed, and production schedules were reassembled. Many shows were expected to produce a limited number of episodes to close out the abbreviated season, while some series canceled the remainder of their runs entirely.

## Oscars Spared

The settlement arrived in time to rescue the 80th Academy Awards ceremony, which had been in jeopardy as the strike dragged on. The Golden Globes had already been reduced to a bare news conference after actors refused to cross picket lines, and organizers feared the Oscars telecast could meet a similar fate.

With the strike resolved, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences proceeded with a full ceremony, complete with its traditional red-carpet arrivals, star presenters and scripted program. The resolution removed the threat of a scaled-back broadcast and allowed the film industry's signature event to go forward as planned.

The end of the walkout brought relief to thousands of behind-the-scenes workers — from set builders to caterers — who had been idled by the shutdown and had gone without pay throughout the dispute.
